1:
The psalm opens not with a precept but with a question flung up to God himself, and the witnesses gather about its two images before a single mark of the citizen is named. The reformed John Gill sets the enquiry against the corruption of mankind painted in the previous psalm, which renders men unfit for God's presence, and is careful what the imagery will and will not bear: by the "tabernacle" is meant neither the human nature of Christ nor heaven itself, but the church of God on earth, for the word rendered "abide" signifies to sojourn or lodge as in an inn, and that will not suit a state which is fixed and immovable. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the whole verse as one weighty enquiry — "Lord, who shall abide in thy tabernacle?" is to ask, let me know who shall go to heaven, not who by name, for that the Lord alone knows, but who by description; and he divides the couplet, taking the tabernacle for the church militant, mean and movable like Moses's tent in the wilderness, and the holy hill for the church triumphant, alluding to the Zion on which Solomon would build. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the same distinction through the Hebrew, hearing in "who shall sojourn" (mi yagur) the migratory tabernacle, type of the militant church that has here no continuing city, and in "who shall dwell" (mi yiscon) the fixed temple, type of the rest that remains for the people of God.

Against this two-storey reading the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott holds that the two terms, though properly the one meaning to sojourn like a passing guest and the other to dwell like a resident, are here used as plain synonyms, the verse asking simply what constitutes a true and genuine citizen of the kingdom of God; and Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, read the psalm as the answer to the previous psalm's longing for a righteous generation, and set it beside Ps. 24, composed when the Ark came up to Zion (cf. 2 Sam. 6:19), though the bare title "holy mountain" inclines them to date it rather to the Absalom exile, when David was cut off from the sanctuary. The latin-fathers Augustine reads the tabernacle spiritually as a thing of war — soldiers, he notes, are called tent-fellows — so that "who shall sojourn" fits the season in which we war with the devil and need a tent to refresh ourselves, while the holy mountain where one shall rest he takes for the eternal habitation, the supereminence of the love of Christ in life everlasting.

The other reformed voice, John Calvin, lifts the verse to the covenant: God chose the Jews and set his sanctuary among them on this condition, that they show themselves a peculiar and holy people by a just and upright life, so that hypocrites who merely occupy the temple in vain pretend to be his people; and David, rather than dispute with men, addresses God, who alone can sift his own from strangers. The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon presses the question deeper still, for on the ground of law no mere man can dwell with the God whom the very heavens are not pure before; the humbled soul would never dare approach were it not for the Advocate who can abide in the heavenly temple because his righteousness endureth for ever. The witnesses do not divide over the drift — that the question searches every worshipper — only over whether its two clauses name two states or one.
2:
The answer opens with three strokes of a single upright life, and the witnesses take them in turn: he "walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart." The reformed John Gill guards the first word against a false rigour, for "uprightly" or "perfectly" does not mean to be without sin, but not to be chargeable with any notorious crime and living in it; perfection here is sincerity, the mark of an Israelite indeed in whom is no guile, whose faith is unfeigned and whose walk is without fraud and deceit. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the very grammar of the reply: the opening distich of question and general answer is now worked out in three tristichs, in clauses that carry the logical force of relative clauses, their perfect tenses bearing the sense of abstract presents — the tried qualities and habitual conduct of the man in view. The other voice of that school, Charles Ellicott, renders the first line "he whose walking is perfect rectitude" (comparing Prov. 28:18), and takes "the truth in his heart" to mean one who both thinks and speaks the truth, setting beside it Shakespeare's counsel, "This above all: to thine own self be true."

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses fill in the three duties. Adam Clarke reads "walketh uprightly" (holech tamim) of the man who sets God before his eyes and takes his word for the rule of his conduct, and "worketh righteousness" (poel tsedek) as giving just weight, rendering to all their dues — to God his heart, to his neighbour the love he owes himself, to his own body and soul their proper care — while "speaketh the truth in his heart" makes him a true man in whom heart, tongue, and hand are all in unison, with no hollow friendships nor empty professions. John Wesley gathers the same into a sentence: to serve God and love his neighbour not in word only but in truth, and that constantly; to make it his business to do justly and give every one his due, first to God and then to men; and to let his words and professions agree with the thoughts and purposes of his heart.

The puritan-evangelical voices press the picture home. Matthew Henry reads the character as one sincere and entire in his religion, walking uprightly according to the condition of the covenant given to Abraham, "walk before me, and be thou perfect" (Gen. 17:1), sound at heart and an Israelite without guile (John 1:47), just to God and man alike, whose very prayers and promises come not out of feigned lips. Charles Spurgeon hears the Holy Spirit answering the question by describing an outward character in which faith, though unnamed, is surely the hidden root; the upright man keeps himself erect as one who walks a high rope or bears fragile ware upon his head, not cringing as a flatterer nor wriggling as a serpent, for walking, he says, is of far more importance than talking, and God's house is a hive for workers, not a nest for drones. The witnesses do not divide: the perfection asked is the perfection of sincerity, proved not in profession but in an upright walk, just dealing, and a truthful heart.
3:
The catalogue turns from a man's own walk to his tongue and his dealings with his neighbour, and the witnesses fasten on the vivid Hebrew behind "he that backbiteth not with his tongue." The reformed John Gill draws the image out of the root, which is that of the "foot": the backbiter is a tale-bearer who goes about from house to house, and the kindred word means spies, so that such men creep into houses, pry into the secrets of families, and divulge them — ranked among the worst of men and unfit for the society of the saints or a church of Christ. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke renders the clause literally, "he foots not upon his tongue," the tongue as it were kicking about the character of an absent man; and he unfolds the English word into a threefold charge, for the backbiter is a knave who would rob you of your good name, a coward who says in your absence what he dared not to your face, and an ill-conditioned dog that flies at your back when it is turned. On the closing clause he weighs the word "reproach" (cherpah), which comes from a root meaning to strip or make bare, as winter (choreph) strips the fields of their clothing: a man of good character is stripped of his fair name by the slander that is carried about, and the good man "taketh it not up" (lo nasa) — he will not bear it, so that the tale dies with him and goes no further.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the picture, rendering "he has not footed it on his tongue," expressive of those who go from house to house carrying tittle-tattle (1 Tim. 5:13), and noting the striking derivation of "reproach" from the stripping of the trees of their autumn fruit — honour and reputation stripped from a person. He marks too that two different Hebrew words stand behind "neighbour," and would translate, "Who does no ill to his friend, nor carries a reproach against his neighbour," expressly setting aside the marginal "receiveth" or "endureth" as quite against the sense. Here a small difference of reading surfaces, for the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley glosses "taketh not up" more broadly — the good man does not raise the reproach, nor spread or propagate it, nor even believe it without sufficient reason — so that where Ellicott would confine the phrase to the carrying of a slander onward, Wesley lets it reach also to the too-ready believing of one.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into the portrait of a man who does all the good he can and hurt to no one, and is in particular tender of his neighbour's good name. He backbites not, defames no man, makes not others' faults the matter of his common talk nor his sport, but frowns upon a backbiting tongue and so silences it (Prov. 25:23); he neither raises a reproach nor receives it, but if an ill-natured story be told him will disprove it if he can, and if he cannot, it shall die with him and go no further, his charity covering a multitude of sins. The witnesses do not divide: the citizen of Zion is known as much by the evil his tongue refuses to carry as by the good his hand performs.
4:
Now the psalm weighs a man not by his fortune but by his loyalties, and the very first clause divides the witnesses over its grammar. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott owns that the line is obscure, its subject and predicate not clearly marked, yet holds the Authorized Version right — "in whose eyes a vile person is contemned" — for it is quite out of keeping with the context to make both verbs predicates and read, "he is despised and rejected in his own eyes," as of one who thinks humbly of himself; the meaning is that those deserving contempt are contemned, while the good who fear Jehovah are honoured. The reformed John Gill records both readings without finally forsaking either: the vile person, a wicked and abandoned creature though he stand in high places, is to be despised by God's people as an abomination to God, as Haman was contemned by Mordecai and Ahab by Elisha; yet he allows that the clause may be rendered of a good man "despised in his own eyes" on account of his own vileness and the imperfection of his obedience, the humble sense of the Targum, Aben Ezra, and Kimchi, and no bad sense, though he thinks the former the better countenanced.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke plays out the same tension. The vile person (nimas), he says, is the reprobate, loathsome (nibzeh) as though covered with leprosy, whom the righteous man must hold in contempt though he be rich, learned, and honourable, for popular odium should ever be pointed against vice; yet Clarke also relays Aben Ezra's curious turn, "he is mean and contemptible in his own eyes," with its beautiful paraphrase that the pious man counts all his good as nothing beside his duty, much as our Lord bids the servant say, "we are unprofitable servants" (Luke 17:10) — only to conclude that the next clause, the honouring of them that fear the Lord, proves Aben Ezra to have mistaken the sense. That next clause the witnesses read as one: the citizen honours the God-fearing man though he lie, with Job, on a dunghill or, with Lazarus, in his sores, valuing character above rank; and John Wesley adds that he loves them though they be mean in worldly condition and differ from him in opinions of lesser moment.

On the oath the witnesses agree in substance and differ over the text. Gill and Wesley take it of a promissory oath kept though it prove to the swearer's own damage — a man must rather suffer loss to himself and his family than wrong his neighbour by breaking it — and Clarke makes the bare word of such a man as binding as his oath, since "he that will not be honest without an oath will not be honest with one." Yet Clarke notes that the Hebrew may be read "he sweareth to afflict himself, and changeth not," as the Chaldee has it, of one who has vowed to keep his body under; and Ellicott reports that the Septuagint, by transposing the letters, read "to his neighbour" rather than "to his own hurt," a thought the old Prayer Book version seems to have combined with the received one. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps to the plain sense and marvels at the strength of the bond, that even wise and good men may swear to their own hurt unawares, and yet an oath is so sacred a thing that it must be kept at a loss rather than played fast and loose with.
5:
The last mark of the citizen touches his purse, and over it the witnesses wage their one real dispute: what exactly the psalm forbids when it praises the man who "putteth not out his money to usury." The reformed John Gill draws the line firmly. To lend to the poor in an extravagant and exorbitant way, biting and devouring their little substance, is the thing condemned; but to lend on moderate interest, according to the laws of nations, is no more unlawful than to take interest for houses and land, for it is common justice that one who lends for another to trade and gain by should share in that gain. The design of the law, Gill says, is to forbid all exactions and oppressions of the poor and to encourage liberality, the covetous who bite and oppress being unfit for church communion. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the same distinction on historical grounds: usury was never forbidden in legitimate dealings with foreigners (Deut. 23:20), and the laws against it looked only to dealings among Israelites and were enacted to protect the poor rather than because interest was in itself wrong (Exod. 22:25; Lev. 25:36); the context here, joined to bribery, limits the sin to its unjust application — the "biting" usury against which every government must legislate — while capital lent for honest trade, as our Lord's parable of the talents shows, was never held averse.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke leans harder on the word itself. Usury, he says, is unlawful interest, got by taking advantage of a distressed neighbour's necessity, and no man that fears God can be guilty of it; the very term (neshech) comes from a root meaning "to bite as a serpent," for the increase, small at first as scarcely to be felt, spreads its venom until it devours another's substance. To this he joins the second clause, "nor taketh reward against the innocent," reading it of the lawyer who, convinced the poor man has right on his side, yet takes the richer fee to plead against him, and so is as sure of hell as if he were already there. John Wesley keeps the plainest and strictest line of all, glossing "usury" simply as lending in a manner contrary to God's law (Exod. 22:25; Lev. 25:36), and "reward" as a bribe for him who has a bad cause — so that where Gill and Ellicott labour to shield honest interest from the charge, Wesley lets the word stand as a plain prohibition.

With the catalogue complete, the witnesses turn to its seal, "he that doeth these things shall never be moved." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry likens such a man to Zion-hill itself, which cannot be removed but abides for ever (Ps. 125:1): every true living member of the church, like the church itself, is built upon a rock, and the grace of God shall always be sufficient to keep him safe and blameless to the heavenly kingdom. Adam Clarke reads the close as the answer to the whole psalm's question, who shall go to heaven — the man who to faith in Christ Jesus adds these moral excellences and so stands fast for ever; and John Wesley hears in "never be moved" the promise that he shall abide with God here, and when he dies be for ever with the Lord. The witnesses do not divide over the seal, only over the reach of the usury it crowns: whether the psalm brands all lending at interest or only the biting usury that preys upon the poor.
